questions.question: National leaders should need to win regular competitive elections to remain in office.
questions.reason: Regular competitive elections make women equal co-authors of government rather than subjects of permanent rulers.

questions.question: National governments should be chosen by a panel of experts rather than by the general electorate.
questions.reason: Expert advice is useful, but substituting an expert panel for citizens denies equal political agency.

questions.question: Every adult citizen should have the right to vote, regardless of their education or intelligence.
questions.reason: Intellectual or educational exclusions would contradict equal citizenship and reproduce unequal opportunities.

questions.question: The head of government should be able to enact national laws even when parliament votes against them.
questions.reason: Constitutional lawmaking and congressional accountability rule out unilateral executive legislation against parliament.

questions.question: Parties opposing the government should be allowed to campaign and stand in national elections under the same conditions as the incumbent government.
questions.reason: Competitive opposition is necessary for meaningful and inclusive electoral choice.

questions.question: Opposition representatives should be able to investigate the government’s use of public money.
questions.reason: Legislative scrutiny of public spending enables accountability for priorities affecting care and equality.

questions.question: Courts independent of the government should be able to overturn government decisions that violate the constitution.
questions.reason: The constitutional civil-rights strategy requires courts able to remedy unlawful governmental decisions.

questions.question: National governments should be chosen by trade union leaders rather than by the general electorate.
questions.reason: Union representation cannot replace the equal political voice of citizens outside organised labour.

questions.question: The governing leadership should have authority to exclude parties from national elections because of their political positions.
questions.reason: Government exclusion of opponents by political position undermines equal participation and competitive choice.

questions.question: Voters should be able to repeal a law through a binding referendum.
questions.reason: Equal citizenship does not establish this particular referendum or recall mechanism. Earlier rationale under review: Binding popular repeal is supported as participation, inferred subject to constitutional equality protections.

questions.question: National leaders should have sole authority over major national policy decisions.
questions.reason: The demand for legislative control of executive action contradicts sole national decision authority.

questions.question: Elected representatives should be able to remove the head of government for serious abuse of power through a defined constitutional process.
questions.reason: The contemporary programme expressly favours impeachment or resignation as constitutional accountability mechanisms.

questions.question: A national leader should be able to postpone scheduled elections without independent approval when they consider political continuity necessary.
questions.reason: A leader deciding when voters may judge them destroys accountable co-authorship of government.

questions.question: Voters should be able to remove an elected representative before their term ends through a defined recall vote.
questions.reason: Equal citizenship does not establish this particular referendum or recall mechanism. Earlier rationale under review: Defined recall procedures can extend voter accountability, provided equal participation and due process are preserved.

questions.question: National leaders should be able to govern without being accountable to voters or elected representatives.
questions.reason: Unaccountable national leadership directly denies citizens political autonomy.

questions.question: The armed forces should be able to replace a civilian government on their own judgement that it is unfit to govern.
questions.reason: Military replacement of civilian government bypasses the constitutional democratic processes used to secure equal rights.

questions.question: Adults should be allowed to make personal choices such as drug use that risk personal wellbeing when they do not directly harm others.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Self-regarding adult choices belong to personal autonomy; support is qualified because addiction can undermine effective choice.

questions.question: Authorities should be allowed to monitor private communications when a court authorises the surveillance to investigate serious crime.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Court-authorised investigation of serious violence can protect autonomy while checking intrusive state power.

questions.question: Peaceful public demonstrations should be allowed even when they temporarily obstruct roads or access to businesses, provided emergency access remains available.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Peaceful collective protest is a means of equal political participation; temporary disruption with emergency access is proportionate.

questions.question: People should be allowed to criticise public institutions, even when their criticism causes widespread offence.
questions.reason: Offence alone cannot justify silencing criticism of the institutions governing citizens.

questions.question: The government should be able to require adults to follow health measures intended primarily to protect those adults themselves.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Paternalistic restrictions primarily protecting competent adults conflict with bodily self-determination.

questions.question: Police should be allowed to keep records of people’s movements for several years, even when those people are not suspected of an offence.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Long-term tracking without suspicion exceeds the targeted protection compatible with privacy and due process.

questions.question: Police should be allowed to stop drivers at random and test them for intoxication, even without a reason to suspect impairment.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: A limited intoxication test protects other road users against concrete harm, unlike policing purely self-regarding conduct.

questions.question: Authorities should be able to restrict a person’s movements before they commit an offence when a court finds a serious risk that they will harm others.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: A court finding serious danger can justify proportionate preventive protection for potential victims.

questions.question: Adults should be allowed to access books, films, and websites that the government considers morally objectionable.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Government moral disapproval does not override adults’ freedom to form their own views and lives.

questions.question: People should be allowed to use online communication services without having to verify their identity with the government.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Private communication without universal state identification supports autonomy, association and safety from coercive exposure.

questions.question: Police should be able to stop and search people without individual suspicion when there is a credible threat of serious violence in the area.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: The opposition to searches without reasonable suspicion favours individualised grounds even in a threatened area.

questions.question: Authorities should be able to prohibit a public gathering when there is credible evidence that it is likely to lead to serious disorder.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: A credible danger creates a genuine balance: protect peaceful assembly while permitting narrowly necessary measures against serious violence.

questions.question: Police should need a court warrant to search someone’s home without their consent, except when there is an immediate threat to someone’s safety.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: A judicial warrant with an immediate-safety exception combines privacy with protection against violence.

questions.question: People should be allowed to publish confidential government information that reveals official misconduct.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Disclosure of official misconduct serves accountability; the inference preserves safeguards for victims’ identifying information.

questions.question: Adults should be allowed to own firearms for personal defence, subject to checks for a history of violence.
questions.reason: Autonomy and equal rights do not settle this particular policing, disclosure, paternalism or weapons trade-off; liberal feminist scholarship records internal disagreement about paternalism. Earlier rationale under review: Self-defence and reducing violence are both autonomy interests; a violence-history check alone does not settle their balance.

questions.question: Authorities should be allowed to hold people suspected of terrorism without independent court review until they consider the threat resolved.
questions.reason: Indefinite detention without independent review contradicts the programme’s explicit due-process commitments.

questions.question: The government should prioritise the national culture over migrant cultures when they conflict.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Equal autonomy judges conflicting practices by their effects on persons, not automatic national-cultural priority.

questions.question: Public services should accommodate different cultural practices, even when doing so requires additional public spending.
questions.reason: Culturally and linguistically competent services can make access substantive, even when accommodation costs money.

questions.question: People who settle permanently in a country should be expected to adopt its cultural customs.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Equal participation does not require adopting every majority custom; basic civic rights and responsibilities still apply.

questions.question: Becoming part of the national community should not require giving up a foreign cultural identity.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Integration into civic life is compatible with retaining a foreign cultural identity.

questions.question: Public institutions should prioritise using the national language over providing services in several foreign languages.
questions.reason: The programme calls for linguistically competent care rather than allowing one-language provision to exclude migrants.

questions.question: National ceremonies should acknowledge Indigenous peoples within the nation, even when they make up a very small share of the population.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Acknowledging Indigenous people follows inclusive civic recognition rather than ranking groups by their size.

questions.question: Government cultural funding should primarily support my country’s predominant traditions.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Equal cultural standing weighs against funding predominately by majority status.

questions.question: Distinct cultural identities should take priority over a shared national culture when their expectations conflict.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Minority identity deserves protection but cannot automatically override common equal-rights obligations; neither blanket priority is accepted.

questions.question: Public institutions should organise their schedules around one common cultural calendar rather than accommodate different communities’ celebrations.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Reasonable scheduling accommodation can preserve equal participation without abandoning all common arrangements.

questions.question: The government should recognise several cultural traditions as part of my country’s national identity.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Recognition of several traditions expresses equal belonging among women of different backgrounds.

questions.question: Integration programmes should encourage migrants to participate in the wider national community rather than live mainly within culturally separate communities.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: The programme seeks full economic and political participation; this supports integration without forced cultural renunciation.

questions.question: Public signage should be written in foreign languages to accommodate migrants within their communities.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Accessible local information can require migrant languages, inferred from linguistically competent public services.

questions.question: Families should give greater emphasis to a shared national identity than to a distinct community identity.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Families’ cultural identification should remain a personal choice rather than a prescribed national hierarchy.

questions.question: Full body coverings, such as the burqa, should remain legal even when other full body coverings are prohibited.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Voluntary religious dress merits accommodation, but a blanket exception to otherwise justified safety restrictions would require a proportionality assessment.

questions.question: My country’s national identity should include several distinct cultural ways of life.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: A plural national identity is consistent with equal inclusion across race, ethnicity and religion.

questions.question: Government integration programmes should emphasise adopting shared national customs rather than maintaining distinct community customs.
questions.reason: Immigrant inclusion and culturally competent health information do not establish this specific national identity, public ritual or integration policy. Earlier rationale under review: Support for integration concerns access and equal rights rather than replacing distinct community customs.

questions.question: Permanent immigration should be subject to a strict annual numerical limit, based on housing availability and workforce deficits.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: A strict cap determined only by housing and labour deficits would neglect family unity and protection needs.

questions.question: People should generally be allowed to settle in another country to improve their living conditions.
questions.reason: Accessible lawful residence and work routes fit the programme’s concern for migrant opportunity and dignity.

questions.question: Only applicants with skills considered important to my country should normally qualify for permanent residence.
questions.reason: Skills-only admission would exclude family members and care workers whose inclusion the programme expressly seeks.

questions.question: Partners and dependent children of immigrants who are permanently settled in my country should generally be allowed to join them.
questions.reason: Improving family reunification directly supports joining settled partners and dependent children.

questions.question: Refugees fleeing their home countries should be allowed to settle permanently, regardless of their skills or cultural compatibility.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: The combination of safe harbour for threatened women and pathways to residence supports durable refugee inclusion beyond skills or cultural fit; permanent status for every refugee is an inference, not an explicit universal promise.

questions.question: People who migrate illegally should be allowed to remain in my country rather than face deportation.
questions.reason: The explicit legalisation programme supports allowing undocumented residents to remain through a fair regularisation route.

questions.question: Permanent immigration should be limited even when employers want to recruit more workers from abroad.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Employer demand should neither control admission nor be ignored; independent migrant rights and public capacity require a balanced decision.

questions.question: Immigration should be reduced to ease pressure on housing and public services, even when additional arrivals would bring economic benefits.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Housing pressure and migrants’ equal opportunity both matter; adequate service investment and entry arrangements must be considered together.

questions.question: Family immigration should count towards the same annual numerical limit as other permanent immigration.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Family reunification is a distinct human interest and should not simply be displaced by employment-based quotas.

questions.question: People with a confirmed job offer should generally be allowed to move to my country for work.
questions.reason: Work permits and pathways to residence support accessible labour migration with enforceable worker rights.

questions.question: Applicants for permanent settlement should need sponsorship from an employer or family member.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Mandatory dependence on an employer or relative can trap women in exploitation, contrary to independent status.

questions.question: Graduating from one of my country’s universities should not, by itself, provide a route to permanent residence.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Education can reasonably support a residence route, while graduation alone need not override other fair eligibility conditions.

questions.question: People fleeing persecution should be allowed to enter and receive protection even when ordinary immigration limits have been reached.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Safe harbour for persecution and violence should not disappear when ordinary admissions quotas are exhausted.

questions.question: The government should prioritise migrants from culturally similar countries.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Preference by cultural similarity conflicts with equal treatment across ethnic and religious backgrounds.

questions.question: My country should allow non-citizen migrants to receive welfare benefits or live in social housing.
questions.reason: Healthcare and safety-net access regardless of status directly support extending basic welfare access to migrants.

questions.question: My country should allow more migrants from diverse backgrounds because their cultures differ from our own.
questions.reason: NOW supports legalization, family unity and protection of migrant abuse victims, but does not settle this question’s distinct quota, capacity, admission or asylum condition. Earlier rationale under review: Cultural diversity is compatible with inclusion, but difference alone is neither a reason to admit nor to exclude a person.

questions.question: My country should be willing to use military force to secure national interests, even when it has not been attacked.
questions.reason: Force for interests without an immediate threat conflicts with the programme’s opposition to aggression.

questions.question: Diplomatic measures should take priority over military action, even when they are slower to achieve my country’s aims.
questions.reason: The foreign-policy resolution explicitly prioritises diplomacy, conflict resolution and peacebuilding.

questions.question: My country should be willing to bear substantial financial costs to maintain military superiority over potential opponents.
questions.reason: Redirecting resources toward communities weighs against paying for superiority as an independent national aim.

questions.question: Military action should be permitted to prevent an imminent attack when there is strong evidence that the attack is being prepared.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: The resolution distinguishes an evidenced immediate threat from unsubstantiated aggression, permitting narrowly defensive prevention.

questions.question: My country should use armed force only to respond to an armed attack against itself or an ally.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Defence against attack is legitimate, but the resolution also recognises immediate threats before an attack; the absolute restriction is too narrow.

questions.question: My country should require male citizens to complete a period of military service to train a large, capable force and deter potential aggressors.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Male-only compulsory service imposes a sex-assigned civic burden and expands militarisation.

questions.question: My country should accept substantial diplomatic concessions to prevent a war, even when doing so weakens its international position.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Substantial diplomatic concessions can be justified to protect civilians and prevent war, subject to basic rights.

questions.question: My country should develop AI-powered weapons that can select and attack targets without a human approving each attack if this would make military operations more efficient and improve national security.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Removing human attack approval raises accountability and civilian-protection concerns that efficiency alone does not resolve.

questions.question: Defence policy should focus on repelling attacks rather than conducting military campaigns abroad.
questions.reason: Defensive protection better fits the emphasis on immediate danger than discretionary foreign campaigns.

questions.question: My country should avoid war and military action at all costs, even if an ally is being attacked.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Avoidance at all costs could abandon people under attack; the programme’s anti-aggression position is not unconditional non-resistance.

questions.question: My country should maintain forces capable of prolonged combat beyond its borders.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Permanent expeditionary capacity diverts resources toward the militarism the programme opposes.

questions.question: My country should leave a territorial dispute unresolved rather than start a war to settle it.
questions.reason: Peaceful continuation of a territorial dispute is preferable to initiating war over it.

questions.question: My country should be willing to threaten military action to obtain concessions in serious international disputes.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Coercive threats can endanger civilians and displace the preferred diplomatic resolution of disputes.

questions.question: When the two conflict, reducing the risk of war should take priority over demonstrating military resolve.
questions.reason: Reducing war risk is the stronger priority where displays of resolve undermine peace.

questions.question: My country should use military espionage to gain an advantage over potential opponents, even when doing so risks worsening relations with them.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Intelligence protecting against an immediate threat can be justified; seeking advantage at the cost of escalation is not a general mandate.

questions.question: My country should accept reductions in its military capabilities as part of negotiated efforts to prevent war.
questions.reason: Opposition to unjustified war does not establish this specific operational policy; an exception to opposition is not positive endorsement of force. Earlier rationale under review: Negotiated capability reductions are consistent with peacebuilding if they preserve adequate protection against aggression.

questions.question: My country’s institutions should have final authority over laws that apply within its borders.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Domestic finality should not immunise violations of internationally recognised human rights.

questions.question: International institutions should have authority to make binding decisions for my country, even when my government opposes those decisions.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Accepted international standards can constrain a government even when its present leadership objects.

questions.question: Courts in my country should have final authority when national law conflicts with an international court’s ruling.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Rights-based international adjudication should not be defeated automatically by contrary domestic law.

questions.question: My country should make long-term commitments to international alliances, even when those commitments limit its freedom to act independently.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Durable cooperation can require reciprocal limits on unilateral freedom, particularly for peace and rights.

questions.question: My country should be able to withdraw from international commitments without needing approval from international institutions.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Democratic consent supports withdrawal, while obligations to other people limit unilateral escape; the procedure depends on the commitment.

questions.question: International courts should have binding authority over disputes involving my government, including cases brought against its own officials.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Accountability for officials is consistent with universal rights and should extend to agreed international adjudication.

questions.question: My country should prioritise its own interests when they conflict with goals set by international institutions.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Human rights are indivisible across borders, so national advantage does not automatically override common goals.

questions.question: Countries should give international institutions decision-making authority over environmental problems that cross national borders.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Shared authority can address cross-border environmental harms affecting equal life opportunities.

questions.question: My country should remain outside international blocs that require members to adopt a common foreign policy.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: A common rights-respecting foreign policy can support collective peace efforts; independence is not sufficient reason for exclusion.

questions.question: International human-rights institutions should be able to require changes to my country’s laws.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: International requirements protecting equal rights can legitimately require domestic legal reform.

questions.question: My country should keep control of its currency rather than transfer monetary policy to a shared international authority.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: National and shared currencies can both serve autonomy and fair distribution; the institutional design and social effects decide.

questions.question: My country should pool funding and decision-making with other countries to manage shared international problems.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Pooling resources for shared problems follows the international dimension of equal rights and human welfare.

questions.question: My country should retain sole authority over entry at its borders rather than share that authority with international institutions.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Protection obligations and migrant rights justify some shared constraints on exclusive border authority.

questions.question: My country should accept common trade rules negotiated with other countries rather than set all its trade rules independently.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Negotiated common rules can make cross-border exchange accountable and predictable, provided equal rights are protected.

questions.question: My country should keep control of national policy rather than join an international political federation.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: A federation and a sovereign democracy can each secure equal political agency; neither institutional scale is intrinsically preferred.

questions.question: My country should join international efforts to enforce collectively agreed rules, even when staying neutral would better serve its immediate interests.
questions.reason: Universal rights and international solidarity do not establish this transfer of binding sovereign powers. Earlier rationale under review: Cooperation in enforcing agreed rights and peace rules can outweigh immediate national advantage, without endorsing every military enforcement proposal.

questions.question: Most businesses in my country should be privately owned.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Equal access to business and professions within a reformed market economy supports a substantial private business sector.

questions.question: Essential utility networks in my country, such as water supply networks, should be publicly owned.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Public utility ownership and regulated private provision can both secure equal access; control, affordability and accountability determine the choice.

questions.question: Private ownership should be preferred when public and private providers could offer comparable cost, quality, and access.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Equal cost and access leave autonomy and accountability relevant; the doctrine gives neither ownership form automatic preference.

questions.question: My country should establish publicly owned businesses in competitive industries rather than leave those industries entirely to private owners.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: A public competitor can remedy exclusion, but establishing one is not intrinsically better than effective regulation and equal access.

questions.question: Healthcare facilities in my country should generally be privately owned, even when treatment is publicly funded.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Affordable reproductive and general healthcare can use either ownership model; a general private-ownership preference does not follow.

questions.question: Passenger rail infrastructure in my country should be publicly owned.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Public rail infrastructure and regulated private infrastructure can both expand opportunity; access and accountability matter more than network title alone.

questions.question: Publicly funded services should be contracted to privately owned providers when they can offer comparable quality and access at lower cost.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: A lower-cost provider with equal quality and access can preserve resources for autonomy-enhancing services, conditional on fair labour standards.

questions.question: My country should have publicly owned banks alongside private banks.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: A public bank could widen credit access, while anti-discrimination and regulation can do so through private banks; the choice is instrumental.

questions.question: My country should sell publicly owned commercial businesses to private owners.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Selling commercial firms may fund equality measures or reduce useful public capacity; support for public care does not itself determine commercial ownership.

questions.question: Public bodies should own a substantial share of rental housing in my country.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Housing equity and survivor security can be pursued through public ownership, regulated private rental or financial assistance; the programme does not privilege a substantial public title share.

questions.question: Businesses important to national security should remain privately owned when government regulation can protect security interests.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Security regulation addresses one interest, while equal access and accountability still determine whether private ownership is suitable.

questions.question: Businesses extracting natural resources in my country should generally be publicly owned.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Resource ownership is judged by fair benefits and environmental costs rather than a categorical public or private presumption.

questions.question: Public bodies should contract routine services, such as waste collection, to privately owned businesses rather than operate their own providers.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Municipal operation and private waste contracts can both satisfy equal service and worker protections; ownership alone does not settle the issue.

questions.question: The government should retain ownership of strategic businesses even when selling them would raise substantial public revenue.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Strategic retention can protect access, while a sale can fund equal opportunity; the balance depends on what public control actually secures.

questions.question: A publicly owned business that repeatedly needs financial support should be sold to private owners rather than kept in public ownership.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: Subsidy needs alone do not establish failure or a case for sale when a service supplies public benefits that markets underprovide.

questions.question: My country should own a national broadcaster rather than leave broadcasting entirely to private owners.
questions.reason: Equal access and opposition to discrimination do not establish an ownership preference among otherwise comparable providers. Earlier rationale under review: A plural media system with an independent public broadcaster can widen political voice beyond commercial purchasing power.

questions.question: My country should use import tariffs to protect domestic businesses from foreign competition.
questions.reason: The cited feminist programme does not specify this trade instrument; nondiscrimination is not a complete trade programme. Earlier rationale under review: Protecting firms solely from competition is weaker justification than remedying demonstrable unequal opportunity.

questions.question: My country should remove most barriers to international trade, even when some domestic businesses lose sales.
questions.reason: The cited feminist programme does not specify this trade instrument; nondiscrimination is not a complete trade programme. Earlier rationale under review: Open exchange can expand opportunity despite particular firms losing sales, with adjustment support and labour safeguards.

questions.question: My government should favour domestic suppliers when purchasing goods, even when foreign suppliers offer lower prices.
questions.reason: The cited feminist programme does not specify this trade instrument; nondiscrimination is not a complete trade programme.
